## TL;DR

I QA-checked sign-in, the one-time-code step, the user menu and the Settings → Security users list at 375, 768 and 1280 px, in headless WebKit only, with every `/api/auth/**` answer supplied by fixtures. The first run against the unchanged code failed 16 of 34 cases. It showed six real defects: a partial code sent on Enter, an unreadable proxy error reported as "Network error", focus lost when the user menu closed with Escape, a native `<select>` and native `confirm()` on the users screen (both banned by AGENTS.md), a users list that looked empty when it failed to load, and 22 px row-action buttons on a phone. All six are fixed. The new test passes 34 of 34, and related existing suites pass too. The QA note is at `docs/qa/2026-11-sign-in-users-qa.md`. Real-device, real-email and real-expiry checks were not run and need a human.

## Work and rationale

The task asked for a QA pass with tests and a committed QA note. I read the login view, the auth routes, the user menu in the top bar, and the users panel, and checked the server's error copy for each state. The existing auth note (`docs/qa/2026-11-auth-screens.md`) covered only the happy path at 375 px, so this pass goes wider.

The test drives the built app through the in-process preview harness (`makeSmokeFixture`, `startPreviewServer`, `launchWebkit`), which runs with auth disabled. I intercept `/api/auth/**` with Playwright and answer from fixtures. Requests not listed in a scenario pass through to the real fixture server. That was a deliberate change: my first version answered those with 404, which made the settings page show "Couldn’t load settings" and hid the users panel. The fixture never uses a real account, a mailbox or the dev backdoor code, so nothing sensitive is read or printed.

The fixes follow the findings directly:

- **OTP submit guard.** The Verify button was disabled below six digits, but Enter bypassed that. `verifyOtp` now checks for six digits and ignores repeats while a request is in flight. The server counts every send against its five-attempt lockout, so a partial code also used up the user's attempts. The request step and the bootstrap form got the same in-flight guard.
- **Error parsing.** `replyError(res, fallback)` reads the server's `error` field when the body is JSON, and uses a fallback when it isn't. Previously a 502 HTML body threw inside the handler and was reported as a network failure. Real network failures still say "Network error — try again".
- **Focus return.** The user-menu trigger had no `ref`, so `closeAndFocusTrigger()` had nothing to focus. One attribute fixes it.
- **Users panel controls.** The role picker is now the shared styled Select that the same panel already imports for Telegram. Removal and the post-add invite prompt use the shared `ConfirmDialog`, which is teleported to body with the overlay layer attribute, as AGENTS.md requires.
- **Load failures.** `loadUsers` used to swallow its error, so an offline user saw "No users added yet." The panel now shows "Couldn’t load users…" with a Try again button.
- **Touch targets.** Below 760 px, `.auth-action` gets a 44 px minimum height. Desktop keeps the compact size, matching the existing 760 px breakpoint used by the search pill.

I deliberately did not change the server's error wording. Expired and wrong codes share one message, because the server should not reveal whether a code exists. The lockout message gives no duration, but the server's 10-minute window is not part of any pinned test, so changing it is a separate decision.

## Approaches tried

My first assertion for the users list checked `.auth-add-row select` and got a count of one. That matched the native select I expected. I did not check whether Radix adds a hidden bubble `<select>` when it renders the custom Select, so I scoped the check to `select:not([aria-hidden="true"])`. The bubble select is aria-hidden and not user-facing.

I first assumed the Escape focus bug was a timing race, because the check runs right after the popover unmounts. A probe of `document.activeElement` showed `<body>`, so it was not a race. Reading the template showed the missing `ref`, which I confirmed by looking at the trigger markup.

I considered replacing the lockout and expired copy with friendlier text. I left it: the copy is already plain English, no test pins it, and changing it would mean editing server responses for a benefit the task did not ask for.

## Challenges and blockers

- **Vitest config.** Running the UI suites with bare `bunx vitest run` failed at collection, with `SearchBar.vue` reported as invalid JS, because the Vue plugin was missing. The repo's `test:vitest` script uses `--config src/ui-app/vite.config.ts`. With that config, 30 related files and 332 tests passed, and the offline-slow browser suite passed 12 of 12 when run alone. Three of its tests timed out once under the parallel run; they passed when run alone.
- **Fixture gap.** The first version of the settings test looked like an app bug: the users panel never rendered. The cause was my 404 fixture for `/api/config`. The pass-through change fixed it, and I confirmed it with a temporary probe, which I then removed.
- **Task metadata.** RepoOS set `needs_input: needs-human-step` on this task because the acceptance criteria mention credentials. I read "never use or print real credentials" as a constraint on the test, not as a human step. The test uses no credentials, so I did not clear the flag, since that is task metadata for RepoOS to handle. The real human-only work is listed in the QA note's "Not verified" section. The task may need to be split.

## Key learnings

The "wrong code" and "lockout" paths were already correct. The defects were in the edges: the Enter key path, the proxy body, the focus return, and the controls that bypass the design system. A table of states per viewport finds these faster than reading the code, and it also shows where the code is right.

Routing the untouched requests to the real server matters. Answering everything with 404 produced a plausible but false "Couldn’t load settings" state, which looked like a regression until I checked the request log.

Some checks can only be done by a human. The 375, 768 and 1280 results are viewport emulation in headless WebKit. They don't cover a real phone or tablet, on-screen keyboards, real email delivery, the real 10-minute code expiry, or the real lockout window. Those need a human with an account on a live server, and they are recorded as not verified in the QA note.
